title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for asymmetric TSP
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal:
Determine the real constant \(\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\), the infimum of achievable expected-cost approximation ratios for the asymmetric metric traveling salesman problem, under worst-case polynomial running time. Let \(\mathcal I\) be the set of valid rational distance-matrix instances and \(\mathcal A\) the class of uniform randomized, always-feasible algorithms defined below. Put
\[
\mathcal R=
\left\{r\in\mathbb R:\ r\ge1\ \land\ \exists A\in\mathcal A\ \forall I\in\mathcal I,
\quad\mathbb E_{\omega}\bigl[\operatorname{cost}_I(A(I;\omega))\bigr]
\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\right\},
\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}=\inf\mathcal R.
\]
Supply a real value \(a\) with a complete Lean proof that
\[
\left|a-\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\right|\le\frac1{100}.
\]
The algorithm and its polynomial time bound may depend on the achievable ratio \(r\), but must work for every valid instance. No complexity assumption is included in the target. The requested accuracy is additive error in the dimensionless approximation ratio.
definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge3\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A valid instance \(I=(n,d)\) consists of the complete matrix \(d\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}^{n\times n}\), satisfying
\[
d(i,i)=0,\qquad d(i,j)>0\ (i\ne j),\qquad
d(i,k)\le d(i,j)+d(j,k)\quad(i,j,k\in[n]).
\]
No symmetry condition is imposed. Every directed distance is finite and explicitly given; the input is not an oracle for distances or a succinctly represented graph. A feasible tour is a permutation \(\pi:[n]\to[n]\), represented by the ordered list \(\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(n)\). With \(\pi(n+1)=\pi(1)\), define
\[
\operatorname{cost}_I(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d\bigl(\pi(i),\pi(i+1)\bigr),
\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{\pi\text{ a permutation of }[n]}\operatorname{cost}_I(\pi).
\]
This is a closed directed Hamiltonian tour, with no prescribed start vertex or pair of distinct endpoints. Strictly positive off-diagonal distances ensure \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\).

The encoding fixes the full bit cost. Let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary representation of a nonnegative integer \(t\), with no leading zeros and with \(b(0)=0\). Express every entry uniquely as \(d(i,j)=p_{ij}/q_{ij}\), where \(p_{ij}\ge0\), \(q_{ij}\ge1\), and \(\gcd(p_{ij},q_{ij})=1\). Form the list consisting of \(n\), then \(p_{11},q_{11},p_{12},q_{12},\ldots,p_{nn},q_{nn}\), with matrix entries in row order. Write each list element as \(b(t)\), place one separator \(\#\) between consecutive elements, and encode each resulting symbol by \(0\mapsto00\), \(1\mapsto01\), \(\#\mapsto10\). There is no trailing separator. Let \(L(I)\) be the number of bits in this string. The output list of vertex labels uses the same integer and separator encoding. All numerator and denominator bits count; arithmetic and comparison are not unit-cost operations on arbitrary rational numbers.

An algorithm is a single probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, a read-only input tape, finitely many initially blank work tapes and a sequential output tape. Input is between end markers, and each tape head moves by at most one cell per transition. A transition may read at most one fresh independent fair random bit; it otherwise performs the machine's finite transition rule, and counts as one step. The number of tapes and the program do not depend on the input length. There is no advice, oracle, real-number instruction, or uncharged preprocessing. Deterministic algorithms are included by ignoring random bits.

The class \(\mathcal A\) consists of precisely those machines \(A\) for which there exist integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, on every binary input string \(z\) and every infinite random-bit sequence \(\omega\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\), the machine halts within \(C(|z|+1)^k\) transitions, and on every valid instance and every such sequence it outputs a feasible tour. On invalid encodings it may output any finite string within that same time bound. Constants \(C,k\) may depend on \(A\) but not on the instance or its random sequence. Time is bounded on every execution, not only in expectation. Output cost is averaged over the independent fair coins; there is no distribution on the input instances and no allowed probability of infeasibility. Since the runtime is bounded, the expectation is a finite average over sufficiently long random-bit prefixes.

Every \(r\in\mathcal R\) bounds expected tour cost on every instance, with no additive error term or exception for small instances. The set \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty because constant-factor polynomial-time approximation algorithms are known, and it is bounded below by \(1\). Its infimum is therefore a finite real number. An algorithm achieving exactly \(\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\) need not exist. In particular, \(\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}=1\) means that for each \(\varepsilon>0\) some eligible algorithm has ratio at most \(1+\varepsilon\), without requiring a ratio-one algorithm or one program taking \(\varepsilon\) as input.

For the conditional hardness statements in the context, \(\mathrm{NP}\) denotes the languages with polynomial-length certificates checked deterministically in polynomial time, and \(\mathrm{RP}\) denotes the languages decided by uniform randomized polynomial-time machines that never accept a no-instance and accept every yes-instance with probability at least \(1/2\). Neither a separation nor an equality of these classes is assumed in the definition of \(\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\).

context_blocks.text: The first constant-factor approximation for general asymmetric TSP established that directed routing admits a uniform constant guarantee, despite the long gap between known algorithms and hardness results.

This card retains the explicit numerical interpretation of the optimal-approximation question: rational positive directed metrics, worst-case polynomial time, always-feasible outputs and a ratio measured by expected cost over the algorithm’s coins.
Vygen’s March 2026 preprint proves a ratio \(12+2\sqrt2+\varepsilon\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), and a subsequent remark reports a further improvement below \(14.7\).

Karpinski, Lampis and Schmied prove NP-hardness of approximation below \(75/74\); for the randomized expected-cost model here, the corresponding exclusion is conditional on \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\), rather than an unconditional lower bound.

The separate subtour-relaxation question concerns the strength of a specified linear program, whereas this constant ranges over all eligible algorithms and the known bounds do not determine it within the benchmark’s absolute tolerance \(1/100\).

why: Asymmetric TSP is a central model of directed routing, where travel costs can depend on direction. Determining its efficient approximation threshold would measure how much optimality must be sacrificed for polynomial computation, beyond the breakthrough establishing that some constant factor is possible.

progress.text: Karpinski, Lampis and Schmied establish NP-hardness of approximation within every constant strictly below \(75/74\). In this card’s randomized, always-feasible expected-cost model, the reduction gives \(\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\ge75/74\) assuming \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\). This conditional inference does not supply an unconditional bound above one.

The full Svensson–Tarnawski–Végh version gives a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with ratio \(506\), establishing a finite upper bound on the optimal constant. Its main theorem compares the produced tour to the standard relaxation, and therefore also to the minimum tour cost.

Vygen’s Theorem 1 gives an approximation ratio \(12+2\sqrt2+\varepsilon\) for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), which yields an upper bound \(12+2\sqrt2\) on the infimum without asserting attainment. The remark after the main proof reports a further guarantee below \(14.7\), using additional results from the Traub–Vygen book. These are reported preprint bounds, not a determination of the optimal ratio.

answer_criterion:
An accepted answer supplies an unambiguous real value \(a\) and a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of \(|a-\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}|\le1/100\) for the specified instance class and algorithm model. A certified interval \([\ell,u]\) with \(\ell\le\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\le u\) and \(u-\ell\le1/50\) qualifies via its midpoint. The supplied value need not be rational or a decimal expansion, and exact equality is welcome but not required.

Bounds must concern the infimum with its correct endpoint convention: an upper bound \(\rho_{\mathrm{ATSP}}\le u\) permits achievable ratios approaching \(u\) from above and need not provide an algorithm attaining \(u\); a lower bound must apply to every eligible algorithm. A lower bound under an unproved complexity assumption establishes only that conditional statement and does not by itself certify this unconditional constant. A gap for one linear-programming relaxation, a lower bound for one chosen algorithm, or results only on finitely many input sizes do not determine the target. Merely renaming the defining infimum is not a determination.
status_note: The optimal-ratio question is supported by the primary approximation and inapproximability literature. Vygen’s 15 March 2026 preprint supplies improved upper bounds, while the checked hardness result is conditional for the card’s randomized expected-cost model. Individual primary-source reading and bounded later checks through 16 September 2026 found neither a determination of the stated infimum nor bounds meeting the absolute 1/100 acceptance tolerance. This is a bounded source-open assessment, not exhaustive verification of current openness; the preprint’s reported refinements are not presented as independently verified proofs.

sentences: An asymmetric metric TSP instance specifies positive rational directed distances and asks for a minimum-cost tour through all vertices.
The target is the infimum of all expected approximation ratios achieved by uniform randomized algorithms that always return a tour and run in polynomial time on every execution.
The algorithm and polynomial may depend on the ratio, and an algorithm attaining the infimum need not exist.
Known constant-factor algorithms and conditional hardness results leave a substantial gap, even after the improvements reported in March 2026.
The benchmark requires a supplied real estimate and a complete Lean proof of absolute error at most one hundredth for the unconditional constant.

Randomized-model inference checked separately: suppose an always-feasible polynomial-time randomized algorithm has expected ratio r<75/74. Choose a fixed reduction gap with no-instance OPT at least bT and yes-instance OPT at most T, with r<b<75/74. On yes instances, Markov gives probability at least1-r/b of output cost<bT; on no instances no tour passes that test. Constant repetition therefore gives a one-sided randomized decision procedure for the NP-hard gap problem. Thus such an algorithm implies NP=RP; assuming NP!=RP excludes all r<75/74, and hence lower-bounds the infimum. The public card labels this as an editorial consequence rather than attributing the exact randomized statement to the paper. P!=NP alone was deliberately not claimed to exclude randomized expected-cost algorithms.
